title: An LLM-Based Multi-Path Question Answering System with XGBoost Routing and Threshold-Based Refusal
authors: Bo Dai; Caiyun Li; Yiyun Cao; Jie Ling; Xiaowen Liu
abstract: In conventional question answering systems, general-purpose large language models (LLMs), despite their strong capabilities in language understanding and generation, exhibit notable limitations in scenarios with stringent factuality requirements. Their outputs often lack explicit evidential grounding, making them prone to hallucinations and inconsistent responses. Moreover, LLMs do not inherently guarantee determinism when performing operations over structured data—such as aggregation, conditional filtering, and cross-field constraints—thereby undermining result consistency and reliability. To address these issues, we propose an internal-data-first framework for controllable question answering in high-risk scenarios. The framework categorizes knowledge sources into unstructured documents and structured data, enabling evidence-constrained generation via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and database-backed, verifiable query execution via restricted, read-only structured queries. In addition, an UNK branch is introduced as a safe degradation mechanism that triggers refusal when inputs lack sufficient evidence, exceed system capability boundaries, or fail to meet confidence requirements, thereby suppressing hallucinations and unauthorized generation. To enable controlled selection among the two execution pathways (RAG/SQL) and the safety degradation branch (UNK) at the system level, we design a learned router based on XGBoost with confidence-thresholded selective prediction, which preferentially activates UNK refusals for low-confidence or out-of-distribution inputs. We validate the proposed framework using a graduate admissions consultation system as an exemplar application, constructing both a document knowledge base and structured score tables, and conducting controlled comparisons across multiple system variants with multi-metric evaluations. Experimental results indicate that, under the current controlled evaluation setting, the proposed framework exhibits relatively stable behavior under complex query formulations and demonstrates practical engineering potential in high-risk vertical-domain question answering scenarios.

title: When Visual Evidence Is Insufficient: How Instructions, Post-Training, and Internal Activations Shape Refusal in Multimodal Language Models
authors: Ananth K Suresh; Aveen Dayal; Gouthaman KV; Aditya Pola; Vineeth N Balasubramanian
abstract: For reliable deployment, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should recognize when an image provides insufficient evidence to answer a question and withhold unsupported answers. Yet refusal alone is not necessarily evidence of such recognition: models may refuse because of unrelated safety constraints or without identifying the missing evidence. We study how refusal on visually unanswerable questions is shaped by three sources of control: inference-time instructions, post-training, and internal activation interventions. Across three MLLMs on the MoHoBench benchmark, we systematically manipulate the meaning and placement of refusal instructions, compare supervised and preference-based post-training, and intervene on a refusal-related activation direction derived from naturally answered and refused examples. We find that refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with model-specific changes at the sample level that are obscured by aggregate refusal rates. Evidence-aware and general refusal instructions have stronger effects than an intentionally mismatched safety instruction. Post-training produces larger increases in refusal, but can also induce responses that combine refusal language with attempted answers. In contrast, activation intervention produces smaller yet transferable changes across prompt conditions, without evidence of indiscriminate refusal on tested visually answerable samples. These findings show that refusal is jointly shaped by external instructions, post-training, and internal representations, highlighting the need to disentangle evidence recognition from a model's learned propensity to refuse.

title: Helping children correctly say “I don't know” to unanswerable questions.
authors: Amanda Waterman; Mark Blades
abstract: Adults ask children questions in a variety of contexts, for example, in the classroom, in the forensic context, or in experimental research. In such situations children will inevitably be asked some questions to which they do not know the answer, because they do not have the required information ("unanswerable" questions). When asked unanswerable questions, it is important that children indicate that they do not have the required information to provide an answer. These 2 studies investigated whether preinterview instructions (Experiment 1) or establishing a memory narrative (Experiment 2) helped children correctly indicate a lack of knowledge to unanswerable questions. In both studies, 6- and 8-year-olds participated in a classroom-based event about which they were subsequently interviewed. Some of the questions were answerable, and some were unanswerable. Results showed that preinterview instructions increased the number of younger children's appropriate "don't know" responses to unanswerable questions, without decreasing correct responses to answerable questions. This suggests that demand characteristics affect children's tendency correctly to say "I don't know." The opportunity to provide a narrative account increased children's appropriate "don't know" responses to unanswerable yes/no questions, and increased the number of younger children's correct responses to answerable questions. This suggests that cognitive factors also contribute to children's tendency correctly to say "I don't know." These results have implications for any context where adults need to obtain information from children through questioning, for example, a health practitioner asking about a medical condition, in classroom discourse, in the investigative interview, and in developmental psychology research.

title: CARE-RAG: Clinically Aligned Risk-Calibrated Evidence-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Safe Medical Question Answering
venue: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
authors: Prudvi Saisaran Ponduru
abstract: Medical large language models can improve access to clinical information, but high-stakes deployment is limited by unsupported claims, retrieval noise, poor citation support, and unsafe over-answering under uncertainty. This paper proposes CARE-RAG, a Clinically Aligned Risk-Calibrated Evidence-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework for medical question answering and clinical decision support. The proposed framework treats answerability control as the central bottleneck in high-stakes medical RAG. It combines risk-tier classification, hybrid retrieval, evidence graph construction, facet coverage scoring, claim-level entailment and contradiction verification, and risk-tiered conformal calibration. The key contribution is an end-to-end decision policy that can answer, redact unsupported claims, or abstain and escalate when evidence is insufficient. The paper presents mathematical formulation, system architecture, algorithms, evaluation protocol, safety governance, reproducibility checklist, and limitations. The manuscript is written as a framework and protocol paper: it does not fabricate clinical trial outcomes, but it specifies a rigorous pathway for empirical validation on public biomedical QA datasets and governed clinical review. The resulting design provides a scholarly foundation for safer, more transparent, and more accountable medical RAG systems.

title: Reliable Indonesian Academic Service Chatbot Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Adaptive Refusal
venue: Jurnal RESTI (Rekayasa Sistem dan Teknologi Informasi)
authors: Jarot Budiasto; Tatik Melinda Tallulembang; Selfina Pare; Muhammad Hasbi
abstract: Academic service information is often stored in lengthy, formal, and distributed university documents, making accurate access difficult. Generative chatbots can improve access but may answer unsupported questions unless retrieval and refusal are controlled. This study proposes a reliability-oriented Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbot for Indonesian academic services integrating BGE-M3, FAISS, adaptive refusal thresholding, rule-based guardrails, Qwen2.5, and retry-on-refusal. A controlled experiment used 12 official documents and 160 Indonesian questions across eight categories. The final configuration achieved Precision@5 of 0.7250, Recall@5 of 0.9125, MRR of 0.8940, nDCG@5 of 0.8888, and mean semantic similarity of 0.8516. All 16 expected-refusal questions were refused and none of the 144 answerable questions was falsely refused, yielding observed refusal accuracy of 1.0000 and a false refusal rate of 0.0000. Retry-on-refusal reduced the false refusal rate from 0.0556 to 0.0000 and increased answerable-only similarity from 0.8150 to 0.8392. These results provide initial evidence that combining retrieval confidence, guardrails, and retry supports more reliable behavior within the controlled benchmark. Because the refusal subset was small and institution-specific, larger evaluations using naturally occurring student queries are required before inferring operational reliability.

title: Evaluating and Mitigating Over-Refusals in LLMs via Task-aware Representation Steering
authors: Utsav Maskey
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive capabilities across diverse tasks including text generation, translation, and question answering. However, their potential misuse for harmful content has led to extensive safety alignment efforts---to make model responses safer (i.e. helpful and harmless). Yet, a fundamental tension exists: harmlessness requires refusing unsafe prompts, while helpfulness demands compliance. Concurrent models rely on safety filters. Consequently, models that heavily rely on exaggerated safety often strike a poor balance, refusing even safe prompts that merely resemble unsafe intent or mention sensitive topics. This thesis investigates the failure mode of over-refusal—the tendency of safety-aligned LLMs to reject benign requests when superficial inputs resemble disallowed content. This work explores this phenomenon across three complementary studies. First, LLM safety on long-tail distributed (encrypted) inputs is analysed: (i) Safety of Instruction Refusal---which examines LLM's tendency to reject harmful obfuscated instructions, and (ii) Generation Safety---which quantifies the suppression of generating harmful responses. This evaluation uncovers early-refusal behaviors, and reveal that aligned LLMs often over-refuse benign tasks or fail to suppress unsafe generation. Building on these findings, secondly task over-refusal is analysed, where LLMs decline responses to harmful instructions, even when they are re-framed as benign tasks (such as sentiment analysis, translation, etc.). Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation'' patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases---and this work introduces "SafeConstellations'', a mechanism that guides representations toward safe and non-refusal pathways when the intention of input task is benign. Thirdly and finally, this thesis extends the over-refusal analysis to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, where both query intent and retrieved context properties influence refusal behavior. Empirical analysis suggest that context arrangement (combination of benign and harmful contexts), domain of query and context, and harmful-text density trigger refusals. Hence, this work extends our prior method to SafeRAG-Steering, that steers embeding regions toward the confirmed safe, non-refusing output regions---reducing refusals in contaminated RAG pipelines. These contributions advance theoretical understanding of over-refusal mechanisms and suggests strategies for deploying safe and controlled language models.

title: Evaluating Retrieval, Grounding, and Refusal in a Citation-Grounded Local RAG Teaching Assistant
authors: Battsetseg Erdenebat; Davaajargal Myagmarsuren; Uranchimeg Tudevdagva
abstract: Learner-centered education requires students to access course knowledge independently while retaining the ability to verify, question, and trace the information provided by AI-supported learning tools. Citation-grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can support this goal by providing on-demand explanations grounded in instructor-approved course materials and by directing learners to the original evidence rather than presenting generated responses as authoritative answers. To examine whether such support can be delivered reliably, this study evaluates retrieval, grounding, citation correctness, and refusal behavior in a locally deployed, citation-grounded RAG teaching assistant for university course materials. The implementation combines OCR-aware ingestion, document- and page-level provenance, sentence-aware chunking, local semantic retrieval, evidence-constrained generation, deterministic refusal normalization, and instructor-facing observability. Two full textbooks, Deep Learning and Power Systems Analysis, were indexed as 2,293 chunks. A source-grounded benchmark contains 60 questions: 52 answerable questions with validated multi-page evidence and eight unsupported questions. With Top-5 retrieval, validated Chunk Hit@5 and Page Hit@5 reached 71.15% and 75.00%, with chunk and page MRR of 0.5135 and 0.5375. Manual evidence-grounded review of end-to-end responses yielded 81.82% normalized correctness among generated answers, 86.36% groundedness, and 86.36% citation correctness. The system answered 42.31% of answerable questions; importantly, 19 of 52 questions (36.54%) were refused even though validated evidence was already present in the retrieved Top-5. Conversely, all eight unsupported questions were correctly rejected with no false answers or citation leakage. The results expose a measurable safety–coverage trade-off: conservative refusal improves unsupported-question safety, but evidence-sufficiency calibration is necessary to avoid suppressing answerable questions.

title: VG-RAG: verification-gated retrieval-augmented generation
authors: G. Kirubavathi; M. Gopi; Vidhun KS
abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factual grounding of large language models by conditioning the outputs based on the retrieved passages. The main drawback of the present Retrieval Augmented Generation model is its implicit nature, where the outputs are based on the retrieved passages. If the passages are not relevant, outdated, or contradictory, the generator will propagate hallucinations before the activation of the correction mechanism. We propose Verification-Gated Retrieval-Augmented Generation (VG-RAG) , where the information retrieved by the system is first sanitized by a deterministic pre-generation verification gate. VG-RAG checks the epistemic qualities of the passage on three fronts: semantic relevance, constraint-aware internal consistency, and corroborative agreement. These are combined using a non-compensatory multiplicative gate that requires all reliability thresholds to be met simultaneously. This prevents any single high-quality signal from overcoming the lack of a signal in other dimensions. Any passage that does not meet these criteria is rejected outright; those meeting the middle confidence criteria are conditionally promoted using an external web-based promotion-only audit. If no passage meets these criteria, the system abstains entirely. We perform experiments with the 150-query HaluEval QA and TruthfulQA benchmarks. The Context Leakage Rate of VG-RAG is 83 % lower than the baseline RAG (0.50 \(\rightarrow\) 0.09 on HaluEval; 0.44 \(\rightarrow\) 0.08 on TruthfulQA), and the Verified Purity of VG-RAG is between 0.70 and 0.85 for the queries for which it returns a response. A falsification test, inspired by the Popperian method, verifies the effectiveness of active adversarial web verification by demonstrating its capacity to falsify 89.3 % of counterfactual claims (95 % CI: 0.83–0.96), while leaving factual statements intact. A controlled ablation study verifies the qualitative distinctness of the failure modes targeted by each of the gate components, as well as the non-compensatory scoring, which is a design choice but also a safety imperative for the retrieval-augmented generation task. Repository : https://github.com/Gopikrish-30/VG-RAG

title: Mitigating Visual Hallucinations in Multimodal Systems through Retrieval-Augmented Reliability-Aware Inference
authors: Pratheswaran Hariharan; Haiping Xu; Donghui Yan
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in vision-language understanding and natural-language response generation. However, these systems can still produce overconfident predictions and hallucination-like outputs, particularly when the visual evidence is weak, ambiguous, or semantically inconsistent. Most existing approaches focus on improving multimodal representation alignment or retrieval-augmented generation, while providing limited mechanisms to quantify instance-level prediction reliability or identify incorrect visual outputs. This work proposes a retrieval-augmented reliability-aware inference framework for trustworthy multimodal visual understanding. The proposed framework constructs an external visual evidence database using pretrained visual embeddings and nearest-neighbor retrieval over normalized feature representations. Retrieved evidence is used to estimate prediction trustworthiness through multiple reliability indicators, including similarity strength, class-support agreement, evidence margin, entropy-based uncertainty, and an aggregate reliability score. Based on these signals, a decision gate determines whether the system should accept the prediction, answer with caution, or abstain/fallback when evidence is insufficient. A multimodal response-generation layer then produces a final user-facing response conditioned on the reliability decision. Experiments on ImageNet-100 demonstrate that the proposed reliability-aware framework improves accepted prediction accuracy from 85.84\% to 88.88\% at 89.04\% coverage. The hallucination-like accepted wrong-answer rate is reduced from 14.16\% to 11.12\%. These results show that integrating retrieval evidence, reliability estimation, and selective decision gating can improve calibration and reduce overconfident visual errors without retraining large multimodal models.

title: SURE-RAG: Sufficiency and Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Verification for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Jingxi Qiu; Zeyu Han; Cheng Huang
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds answers in retrieved passages, yet relevance does not guarantee sufficiency: a topical passage may still fail to justify the answer. We study evidence sufficiency verification for selective RAG answering, in which a verifier receives a question, a candidate answer, and retrieved evidence and decides whether the evidence supports, refutes, or is insufficient for the answer, answering only when support is established. We present SURE-RAG, an aggregation protocol that treats evidence sufficiency as a set-level property: missing hops and unresolved conflicts cannot be detected by scoring passages independently. A shared claim-evidence verifier produces a local relation distribution for each (claim, passage) pair, which SURE-RAG aggregates into four interpretable answer-level feature blocks (coverage, relation strength, uncertainty, and retrieval), producing a three-way decision and an auditable selective score. We evaluate on HotpotQA-RAG v3, a controlled multi-hop benchmark, under an artifact-aware protocol (shortcut baselines, counterfactual swaps, no-oracle checks, and GPT-4o audits). Calibrated SURE-RAG attains 0.9075 Macro-F1 (raw 0.8951 +/- 0.0069), well above DeBERTa mean-pooling (0.6516) and a GPT-4o judge (0.7284), and on par with a strong concat cross-encoder (0.8888 +/- 0.0109) while remaining fully auditable. At 30% coverage, risk falls from 0.2588 to 0.1642, a 37% relative reduction. As a boundary-mapping experiment, we contrast SURE-RAG with GPT-4o on HaluBench unsafe detection: the ranking reverses (0.3343 vs. 0.7389 unsafe-F1), indicating that controlled sufficiency verification and natural hallucination detection are distinct problems.

title: Answerability in Retrieval-Augmented Open-Domain Question Answering
authors: Rustam Abdumalikov; Pasquale Minervini; Yova Kementchedjhieva
abstract: The performance of Open-Domain Question Answering (ODQA) retrieval systems can exhibit sub-optimal behavior, providing text excerpts with varying degrees of irrelevance. Unfortunately, many existing ODQA datasets lack examples specifically targeting the identification of irrelevant text excerpts. Previous attempts to address this gap have relied on a simplistic approach of pairing questions with random text excerpts. This paper aims to investigate the effectiveness of models trained using this randomized strategy, uncovering an important limitation in their ability to generalize to irrelevant text excerpts with high semantic overlap. As a result, we observed a substantial decrease in predictive accuracy, from 98% to 1%. To address this limitation, we discovered an efficient approach for training models to recognize such excerpts. By leveraging unanswerable pairs from the SQuAD 2.0 dataset, our models achieve a nearly perfect (~100%) accuracy when confronted with these challenging text excerpts.

title: Confidence-Gated Semantic Retrieval for Indonesian Customer-Service Intent Classification
venue: JOMLAI Journal of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence
authors: Marco Julius Andreas Bakkara; Mashelina Mashelina
abstract: Customer-service chatbots deployed in low-resource languages must decide not only which intent a message expresses but also when to decline answering. This study evaluated a confidence-gated retrieval architecture for Indonesian intent classification in which a deterministic keyword layer, a multilingual sentence encoder, and an explicit abstention rule were combined. A corpus of twenty-two intents containing three thousand nine hundred sixty training patterns and one thousand fifty-six held-out test patterns was constructed, covering commerce enquiries, complaint handling, and instrumentation engineering questions. Two retrieval backends were compared under identical decision logic: a lexical backend that fused word and character term weighting with a naive Bayes component, and a semantic backend built on multilingual sentence embeddings. The semantic backend reached an accuracy of 82.67 percent and a macro-averaged F-measure of 83.04 percent, exceeding the lexical backend by 11.74 and 12.31 percentage points, at a mean response latency of 30.66 milliseconds on a single processor. Raising the confidence threshold increased selective accuracy from 71.06 to 82.82 percent while coverage fell to 61.17 percent, which quantified the price of caution. Of 100 balanced out-of-scope probes, 93 were rejected (93.00 percent). The deterministic layer resolved just over half of the queries and carried the higher accuracy of the two decision paths.

title: Trusted Uncertainty in Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Confidence Calibration and Risk-Controlled Refusal
authors: Markus Oehri; Conti, Giulia; Kaviraj Pather; Rossi, Alexandre; Serra, Laia; Adrian Parody; Rogvi Johannesen; Petersen, Aviaja; Arben Krasniqi
abstract: Deployed language models must decide not only what to answer but also when not to answer. We present UniCR, a unified framework that turns heterogeneous uncertainty evidence including sequence likelihoods, self-consistency dispersion, retrieval compatibility, and tool or verifier feedback into a calibrated probability of correctness and then enforces a user-specified error budget via principled refusal. UniCR learns a lightweight calibration head with temperature scaling and proper scoring, supports API-only models through black-box features, and offers distribution-free guarantees using conformal risk control. For long-form generation, we align confidence with semantic fidelity by supervising on atomic factuality scores derived from retrieved evidence, reducing confident hallucinations while preserving coverage. Experiments on short-form QA, code generation with execution tests, and retrieval-augmented long-form QA show consistent improvements in calibration metrics, lower area under the risk-coverage curve, and higher coverage at fixed risk compared to entropy or logit thresholds, post-hoc calibrators, and end-to-end selective baselines. Analyses reveal that evidence contradiction, semantic dispersion, and tool inconsistency are the dominant drivers of abstention, yielding informative user-facing refusal messages. The result is a portable recipe of evidence fusion to calibrated probability to risk-controlled decision that improves trustworthiness without fine-tuning the base model and remains valid under distribution shift.

title: VERIBRIEF: A MULTI-AGENT RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION SYSTEM FOR POLICY DECISION SUPPORT
venue: UNM’s Digital Repository (University of New Mexico)
authors: Imane Bahji
abstract: VeriBrief is a multi-agent retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system for evidence-grounded economic policy analysis. The system orchestrates a five-stage LangGraph pipeline, retrieval, research, analysis, synthesis, and critique, to produce cited, structured responses while detecting out-of-scope queries. An empirical evaluation on eight questions drawn from official U.S. macroeconomic releases compared VeriBrief against a single-pass RAG baseline. The multi-agent system achieved 100% refusal precision on unanswerable analytical queries versus 0% for the baseline. Unsupported claims fell substantially on answerable factual questions. A context-propagation defect discovered during evaluation was diagnosed and corrected. Limitations include failure of the evidence gate on policy-counterfactual queries and a regression in unsupported claim rate on policy-template output. Directions for future work are discussed.

title: MTRACE: Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Temporally Diverse Text Corpora
authors: Souhail Bakkali; Anthony Mudet
abstract: Large multilingual knowledge bases expose temporally diverse information, yet retrieval quality remains sensitive to lexical variation and cross-lingual terminology shifts. We develop and evaluate MTRACE (Multilingual Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation with evidence grounding), a pipeline designed to test whether query expansion and multi-query fusion mitigate vocabulary mismatch in temporally layered text corpora, on the French and English subsets of MIRACL. Our approach integrates: (i) semantic query expansion (SQE) and multi-query fusion via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), targeting retrieval stability under query variation; (ii) a generation prompt enforcing strict grounding in retrieved evidence and explicit abstention when evidence is insufficient; and (iii) a modular architecture enabling systematic component evaluation. Ablation studies on Named Entity Recognition (NER) and embedding model selection demonstrate the importance of syntactic coherence in entity extraction and of self-retrieval and efficiency measurements for retriever selection. Our end-to-end evaluation over 50 constructed queries shows faithful answers for well-supported queries, correct abstention on unanswerable questions, and no re-scored similarity gains from multi-query fusion over single-query dense retrieval. By scoping our claims to a clean, text-only baseline, we separate these effects from OCR-noise confounds; direct measurement of diachronic lexical drift is left to future work. Code and configurations are available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MIRAGE-8EAA/

title: RAGGlass: Beyond the Black Box — A User-Centric Glass Box Framework for Inspecting and Diagnosing Retrieval- Augmented Generation
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: khushboo pingle
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates factual hallucinations in Large Language Model (LLM) workflows by extracting corroborating passages from an external corpus prior to response synthesis. Nevertheless, conventional production pipelines operate as opaque black boxes, obscuring intermediate operations such as text ingestion, sliding-window chunking, vector embedding, similarity indexing, and context curation from end users, which impairs their ability to verify underlying evidentiary support. Although modern observability platforms provide extensive diagnostic instrumentation, they cater almost exclusively to engineering telemetry and developer debugging rather than user-facing inspection. This paper presents RAGGlass, a user-facing framework for improving transparency and interpretability in RAG-based question-answering systems. RAGGlass provides an interactive representation of the RAG workflow through seven observable process states and enables configuration of chunk sizes (100–2,000 characters), chunk overlap (0–500 characters), and Top-K retrieval (1–10). It exposes generated chunks, embedding metadata, 384-dimensional representations from all-MiniLM-L6-v2, and retrieved contexts with similarity and distance scores, including live cosine-similarity comparisons between chunks. ChromaDB supports vector storage and semantic retrieval, while response generation uses the Groq API and Ollama for cloud and local deployment. Evaluated on a 17-question test set (14 answerable, 3 unanswerable probes) across seven chunk sizes (200–800 characters) at Top-K=3, RAGGlass achieved 94.12% accuracy (16/17) for chunk sizes 200, 300, and 500, and 100% (17/17) for sizes 400–800. Faithfulness was 100% across all configurations: all unanswerable probes were correctly declined, and the single accuracy failure was an honest refusal. Chunk-level inspection revealed that smaller chunks split answer sentences across boundaries; increasing Top-K fully recovered performance. RAGGlass thus maintains strong question-answering performance while making retrieval evidence and failure modes directly inspectable to users.```[cite: 3]

title: DeclineCraft: A RAG Abstention Benchmark for Jointly Measuring Combined Retrieval and Parametric Knowledge
authors: Atharva Thakur; Abulhair Saparov; Bruno Ribeiro
abstract: Reliable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires recognizing when neither retrieved documents nor parametric knowledge supports an answer. We introduce DeclineCraft, a dynamic abstention benchmark whose unanswerable questions target Minecraft feature additions after a corpus cut-off, with audits of possible parametric exposure. Later cut-offs support evaluation of future models. Across 27 LLMs, we measure Correct Abstention Rate (CAR; how often models acknowledge insufficient knowledge on unanswerable questions), Answerable Attempt Rate and Answer Accuracy. We find that (1) single-shot retrieval significantly raises CAR in 38 of 40 configurations (model and thinking setting) versus no retrieval. (2) Iterative RAG, in which the model self-assesses its context and can request up to two further retrieval rounds, significantly lowers CAR versus single-shot RAG in 30 of 40 configurations (mean 46.4%), with little change in Answer Accuracy (68.5% to 69.3%). Adding query rewriting and reranking to hybrid (dense & sparse) retrieval lowers CAR for all 12 models tested. (3) Larger models answer more accurately (Spearman $ρ= +0.60$ with total parameters), but neither model size nor release date shows a significant association with CAR. (4) Without retrieval, enabling thinking on the same weights lowers CAR significantly for 8 of 13 models (by 14% points on average), and the responses shift from acknowledged uncertainty to premise denial.

title: Condence, Calibration, and Abstention in Small Open-Weight Language Models on Psychiatric Knowledge Questions: A Cross-Domain Replication
authors: Kunal Dhanda
abstract: Abstract Small, locally deployable language models are increasingly proposed for psychiatric clinical decision support on privacy and compute grounds; two contemporaneous 2026 systems (ClinMPO; PKFAR) report accuracy or reasoning-quality gains from augmenting such models, and a 120-study taxonomy of LLMs in mental healthcare lists calibration as an evaluated dimension in none of the studies it covers. A separate, contemporaneous study (Boie et al., 2026) evaluates verbalized-condence cali- bration across 20 medical specialties using six proprietary frontier models on MedMCQA, and a third (Bentegeac et al., 2025) shows across several medical QA benchmarks that verbalized condence is a weak predictor of correctness (AUROC 0.520.68) compared to token probability (AUROC 0.710.87). We narrow the open question this leaves for small, open-weight models specically to psychiatry, using the identical four-model ladder (1.2B9.2B parameters, Ollama, fully local) and harness as a companion general-medicine pilot, on 150 psychiatric-knowledge multiple-choice items (MedMCQA, subject = Psychiatry). Accuracy is higher than on the general-medicine benchmark (57.375.3% vs. 47.763.2%, though at n = 150 the per-model standard error is ±3.54.0 points), and the accuracy ranking partially reorders most notably the 4.3B model falls from 3rd of 4 in general medicine to last in psychiatry. Verbalized condence remains poorly informative about correctness as a ranking signal (AUROC 0.4900.645; one model, the 4.3B, is statistically indistin- guishable from chance) and severely miscalibrated in the aggregate sense (ECE 0.1480.378, well above the 0.0410.141 range Boie et al. report for proprietary frontier models on the same under- lying benchmark family). A naive, unpaired accuracy on answered items framing suggested that oering an abstention option modestly beneted three of the four models. A same-item paired analysis (McNemar's test, bootstrap condence intervals on paired accuracy, and an explicit A→B outcome-transition table) overturns most of that: only the smallest model (1.2B) shows a paired eect distinguishable from noise, and it is negative (−6.7 points, 95% CI [−12.7,−0.7]) repli- cating, point estimate for point estimate, the same model's paired eect on the general-medicine benchmark (−6.7 points, 95% CI [−10.6,−2.5], n = 480). The model with the best condence- ranking signal of the four (7.6B, AUROC 0.645) shows the worst-targeted self-chosen abstentions 8 of its 12 abstentions forfeited an item it would otherwise have answered correctly and its paired eect reverses from a naive +0.8 to a signicant −5.3 points (95% CI [−9.3,−1.3]). We 1read the surviving evidence as: miscalibration and weak error-detection are general properties of this model family; accuracy ranking is domain-dependent and should not be assumed to transfer; and a prompted abstention option is not a free safety improvement for any of the four models once evaluated with paired, coverage-aware statistics rather than naive answered-item accuracy. This is a pilot. n = 150 on a single benchmark family, no clinician adjudicated any output, and MedMCQA multiple-choice measures psychiatric knowledge recall, not psychiatric clinical decision-making. Read as hypotheses for a larger, clinician-involved study, not deployment guidance.

title: When Is Enough Evidence Enough? Sufficiency Judgments and Stopping Rules in Multi-Step Retrieval Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Garvit Kaushik
abstract: A retrieval agent that searches in several steps must decide when it has seen enough. We let two Gemini models retrieve for five steps over a BM25 index and, after every step, state whether the evidence suffices, how likely that is, and their current answer. Logging every step lets us replay any stopping rule offline from one run per model. On 500 HotpotQA and 500 MuSiQue questions we ask how often "enough" is true, whether the judgement predicts a correct answer, and which rule gives the best accuracy for the retrieval spent. Stopping at the first "sufficient" verdict uses 34 to 67% fewer steps than always taking five, at an answer-F1 cost that is not significant in three of four model and dataset pairs and about 0.025 in the fourth. Model choice moves F1 by 0.07 to 0.26, far more than any rule. Against "all gold paragraphs retrieved" the verdict is right 65 to 93% of the time, but a read of 50 apparent premature stops found about 7 in 10 already answerable from the retrieved text, so gold coverage understates it. A dense retriever (small model only) gives the same picture with larger savings. Stated probabilities sit near 0 and 1 and are poorly calibrated; much of their apparent power to predict correctness comes from answers that abstain, and on answered steps the small model's probability is no better than chance. Technical report, not peer reviewed. Code, logs and all numbers: https://github.com/garvitkaushik-123/evidence-sufficiency-agents

title: Evidence-Gated Generative AI: A Reliability-Oriented Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Enterprise Knowledge Systems
venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science Engineering and Technology
authors: Prudvi Saisaran Ponduru; Pavani Priya Vyshnavi Nandanavanam; Sai Kesav Kumar Ponduru
abstract: Large language models can generate fluent answers even when the available evidence is incomplete, stale, contradictory, or outside the user’s authorization boundary. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces dependence on parametric memory, but a retrieved passage is not automatically trustworthy and a generated answer is not automatically supported by the passage that accompanies it. This paper proposes Evidence-Gated Generative AI (EG-GAI), a reliability-oriented architecture that separates answer generation from authorization to release the answer. EG-GAI introduces an evidence ledger carrying source authority, freshness, version and access metadata; claim-level support and contradiction analysis; an Evidence Sufficiency Vector; corrective retrieval for weak evidence; and a tri-state release gate that can release, qualify, or abstain. The architecture is model- and cloud-provider-neutral and is intended for enterprise knowledge assistants, operational copilots, document intelligence, and other high-consequence retrieval-grounded applications. A controlled failure-injection study isolates the retrieval and evidence-control layer using 1,640 documents, 2,600 factual queries, and five equally represented conditions: clean retrieval, irrelevant-document injection, stale-document dominance, peer-quality conflict, and missing evidence. In this controlled corpus, a simple top-1 RAG baseline answered every query but produced a 45.12% unsupported-release rate. Metadata-aware reranking reduced that rate to 13.42%. The full EG-GAI gate released 64.92% of queries, achieved 100% selective accuracy among released answers, and produced no unsupported releases in the controlled study; the absolute unsupported-release reduction versus top-1 RAG was 45.15 percentage points with a 95% bootstrap interval of 43.27-46.96 points. These numbers measure the evidence-control mechanism rather than end-to-end LLM factuality, and therefore are not presented as a benchmark result for any specific language model. The results support the central systems claim: in enterprise Generative AI, generation and release authorization should be distinct decisions, and abstention should be treated as a normal reliability outcome rather than a failure of the interface.

title: Evidence Sufficiency and Safe Degradation of Multimodal AI for Operational Tropical-Cyclone Briefing
authors: Yang You
abstract: When the operational evidence behind a meteorological conclusion is missing, stale, temporally mismatched, spatially mismatched, or conflicting, how does multimodal-AI tropical-cyclone briefing degrade — and can claim-level evidence-sufficiency gating convert unsupported assertions into appropriately qualified answers or abstentions? We combine (1) a fully preserved real-world deployment failure (Typhoon Dolphin, 2026) as a motivating case, (2) a controlled evidence-perturbation testbed (five meteorologically-typed defect families, 26 registered perturbation cells), and (3) multi-storm replication (2023–2026, 8–15 western-North-Pacific storms) with a prospective operational arm. Evaluation is three-dimensional (evidence support; meteorological correctness against observational verification references; epistemic action against an expert-frozen gold standard) with a deterministic claim auditor validated against blinded human annotation. All instruments, case selection, tooling, and analysis rules are frozen in this registration before gold-standard freezing and before any model execution.

title: Search Engines Never Say No: How Frozen Agents React When the Retrieval Tool Refuses
authors: Ramraj Chandradevan; Sayontan Ghosh; Vinoth Selvendran
abstract: A search tool never says no: it returns its top-k passages even when the index holds no answer, so the agent sees irrelevant text instead of a miss signal. We ask what frozen search agents do when the tool refuses instead. On an index-hole testbed (257 NQ and 300 HotpotQA questions run with and without their gold passages in a 21M-passage BM25 index), seven agents receive one of five refusal wordings. An un-announced one-sentence refusal raises abstention on unanswerable questions from 23% to 97% on average for Qwen3-8B/32B and from 28% to 57% for Claude Haiku 4.5, cutting wrong answers almost one-for-one and beating a system-prompt instruction by 51 points on average. Search-R1 ignores the refusal and fabricates retrievals; Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 answer from memory (abstention +2 points) and obey a system-prompt directive instead (+16). We also found that wording matters: an explanation beats a bare token; a directive inside the observation is decisive for Haiku; a soft warning is useless. Realistic triggers, from a lightweight score-based predictor to an LLM grounding judge, fall well short of the oracle, and all land on a benefit-versus-signal-quality curve that prices any trigger by its recall at a fixed false-refusal budget: for compliant agents the bottleneck is the detector inside the tool, not the agent, and the curve tells future detector work what each point of recall is worth.

title: Budgeted Multi-Hop Retrieval Agents with Evidence-Chain Reliability and Cost-Aware Abstention
venue: Journal of Knowledge Learning and Science Technology
authors: Caleb Kong
abstract: Fixed top-k retrieval spends the same context budget on every question without indicating whether a multi-document evidence chain is complete. This study evaluates a budgeted agent on MultiHop-RAG using all 609 documents and 2,556 questions. The 1,534/511/511 train/validation/test split kept each evidence group in one partition. The pipeline compared BM25, 256-dimensional latent-semantic retrieval, equal and weighted reciprocal rank fusion, supervised reranking, fixed depth, and calibrated dynamic stopping. A sparse reader, null detector, and isotonic calibration supported answer, evidence, citation, cost, and abstention evaluation. On 451 answerable test questions, reranking achieved 0.9069 Recall@10, 0.8064 nDCG@10, and 0.7428 complete-chain retrieval. The dynamic agent used a mean of 544.16 tokens and obtained 0.6184 F1, compared with 666.29 tokens and 0.6243 F1 for the null-gated Reranker-8 policy. Its paired F1 difference was -0.0059 with a 95% cluster-bootstrap interval of [-0.0246, 0.0115], while the 122.13-token reduction remained significant after Holm adjustment. Isotonic calibration reduced expected calibration error from 0.2671 to 0.0321. Selective answering operated at 0.3326 coverage and 0.2200 exact-match risk. Snippet retention and citation precision, rather than candidate generation alone, limited joint reliability. The results establish a measured quality-cost trade-off and identify where deeper retrieval still fails to improve answers.

title: Never the Number: Structural Abstention for AI Systems Whose Answers Are Consumed as Fact
authors: Zhelun; Wu
abstract: Large language models have made natural language interfaces to databases (NLIDB) newly credible, but LLM text-to-SQL systems fail in a way that matters for deployment: a hallucinated column or a mis-aggregated total yields a fluent wrong answer, indistinguishable at the point of use from a right one. Where the consumer cannot inspect the generated query, as in enterprise AI deployments and operational dashboards, and increasingly where the consumer is a tool-using agent rather than a person, accuracy alone is insufficient: nothing marks which answers to distrust. This is a reliability problem before it is an accuracy problem. We propose an architectural pattern for such systems, a trusted kernel with a generative shell, resting on one invariant: a component that can fabricate may influence which question the system answers, never which value it returns. A generative shell interprets underspecified input and phrases replies; a deterministic kernel matches fully specified questions against a bounded set of answerable question shapes and compiles them to queries by deterministic execution. The two meet at a confirmation the user reads before any value is computed, and requests the kernel cannot express are declined rather than approximated. We call this structural abstention, and distinguish it from the statistical abstention of selective prediction and calibrated confidence: refusal here needs no confidence estimate, because unanswerable requests are unrepresentable. We specify the pattern implementation-independently, give a five-decision recipe and work it across three domains, extend the invariant from returned values to the actions of agentic systems, and report a two-year production case study alongside two generative alternatives, a fine-tuned parser and a tool-retrieval agent. We close against enterprise and reliability benchmarks published since.

title: UR-RAG: Unified Risk Calibration for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Satyam Mittal; MOHAMED E. FARAG; Miao Lu
abstract: Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation fails when retrieval surfaces weak evidence, when generation misuses adequate evidence, or both, but most abstention methods focus primarily on the generator. We propose UR-RAG, a deployment controller that fuses four runtime signals (retrieval decisiveness, semantic entropy, cluster agreement, and answer support) into one closed-form max-aggregation score, calibrates a shipping threshold against unconditional shipped risk Pr(fail ∧ ship) via a Hoeffding upper-confidence rule, and routes each query through a cheap-then-expensive cascade. Unlike learned-fusion baselines which train a separate parametric head, UR-RAG sets its four channel weights from the same proxy failure labels CRC already consumes and no extra correctness annotations are required. We compare UR-RAG to an 8-feature learned-fusion (LF) logistic baseline on the same signals and the same conformal threshold under a K=5 cross-fit over 13 cells where each cell is a unique combination of dataset, retriever, and cheap-to-expensive generator pair (datasets: TriviaQA, SQuAD, HotpotQA, NQ-open). Three empirical patterns are most relevant: (i) We find that a single cheap-tier weight vector transfers across all nine single-hop cells. Leave-one-cell-out auto-tuning produces the cheap-tier vector (0.25, 0.25, 0, 1.0) across all 9 single-hop cells, with zero weight on cluster-agreement throughout. (ii) The cost of avoiding an additional learned correctness head is small. Within-distribution transfer trails per-cell LF by an average of 0.79 percentage points (pp) in area under the curve (AUC) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of [0.45, 1.16] pp. The pooled-fit LF performs nearly the same as per-cell LF, suggesting the gap reflects the cost of forgoing correctness supervision. (iii) The cascade ships ~80% of shipped answers from the cheap tier and uses ~62% of always-Tier-2 token cost, while every shipping decision is attributable to a single channel and the deployment artifact is a ~200-byte JSON per tier. UR-RAG complements rather than replaces learned fusion: it trades a small AUC margin for label-free weight selection, per-channel auditability at inference, and cross-cell weight transfer. The source code is available at: https://github.com/CMU-AGAI/urrag-hallucination-detection.

title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
authors: Yibo Zhao; Zhu, Jiapeng; Zichen Ding; Xiang Li
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) integrates external knowledge to enhance Large Language Models (LLMs), yet systems remain susceptible to two critical flaws: providing correct answers without explicit grounded evidence and producing fabricated responses when the retrieved context is insufficient. While prior research has addressed these issues independently, a unified framework that integrates evidence-based grounding and reliable abstention is currently lacking. In this paper, we propose GRACE, a reinforcement-learning framework that simultaneously mitigates both types of flaws. GRACE employs a data construction method that utilizes heterogeneous retrievers to generate diverse training samples without manual annotation. A multi-stage gated reward function is then employed to train the model to assess evidence sufficiency, extract key supporting evidence, and provide answers or explicitly abstain. Experimental results on two benchmarks demonstrate that GRACE achieves state-of-the-art overall accuracy and strikes a favorable balance between accurate response and rejection, while requiring only 10% of the annotation costs of prior methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/YiboZhao624/Grace..

title: LatentRefusal: Latent-Signal Refusal for Unanswerable Text-to-SQL Queries
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL (Findings of ACL)
authors: Xuancheng Ren; Shijing Hu; Zhihui Lu; Jiangqi Huang; Qiang Duan
abstract: In LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems, unanswerable and underspecified user queries may generate not only incorrect text but also executable programs that yield misleading results or violate safety constraints, thus posing a major barrier to safe deployment.Existing refusal strategies for such queries either rely on output-level instruction following, which is brittle due to model hallucinations, or on estimating output uncertainty, which adds complexity and overhead.To address this challenge, we first formalize safe refusal in Text-to-SQL systems as an answerability-gating problem, and then propose LATENTREFUSAL, a latentsignal refusal mechanism that predicts query answerability from intermediate hidden activations of an LLM.We introduce the Tri-Residual Gated Encoder (TRGE), a lightweight probing architecture, to suppress schema noise and amplify sparse, localized question-schema mismatch cues that indicate unanswerability.Extensive empirical evaluations across diverse ambiguous and unanswerable settings, together with ablations and interpretability analyses, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme and show that LATENTREFUSAL provides an attachable, efficient safety layer for Text-to-SQL systems.Across four benchmarks, LATENTREFUSAL achieves an average F1 of 88.5% and 88.8% on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-3-8B respectively, while adding ∼2ms probe overhead.

title: LatentRefusal: Latent-Signal Refusal for Unanswerable Text-to-SQL Queries
authors: Xuancheng Ren; Shijing Hu; Zhihui Lu; Jiangqi Huang; Qiang Duan
abstract: In LLM-based text-to-SQL systems, unanswerable and underspecified user queries may generate not only incorrect text but also executable programs that yield misleading results or violate safety constraints, posing a major barrier to safe deployment. Existing refusal strategies for such queries either rely on output-level instruction following, which is brittle due to model hallucinations, or estimate output uncertainty, which adds complexity and overhead. To address this challenge, we formalize safe refusal in text-to-SQL systems as an answerability-gating problem and propose LatentRefusal, a latent-signal refusal mechanism that predicts query answerability from intermediate hidden activations of a large language model. We introduce the Tri-Residual Gated Encoder, a lightweight probing architecture, to suppress schema noise and amplify sparse, localized cues of question-schema mismatch that indicate unanswerability. Extensive empirical evaluations across diverse ambiguous and unanswerable settings, together with ablation studies and interpretability analyses, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and show that LatentRefusal provides an attachable and efficient safety layer for text-to-SQL systems. Across four benchmarks, LatentRefusal improves average F1 to 88.5 percent on both backbones while adding approximately 2 milliseconds of probe overhead.

title: Citation-Enforced RAG Architecture for Decision Support
venue: Encuentro Internacional de Educación en Ingeniería
authors: Imane Bahji; Manel Martínez Ramón; Ramiro Jordán
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed for institutional document synthesis and other reasoning-adjacent tasks. However, hallucinated content becomes an institutional risk when it is incorporated into briefs, policies, or reports. We present a local-first, corpus-restricted retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that enforces a system-level epistemic boundary through three mechanisms: (i) a strict offline corpus boundary, (ii) a traceability contract that requires factual claims to be supported by citations in a structured schema, and (iii) evidence-gated refusal when supporting evidence is weak or absent. We compare a single-pass RAG baseline with a multi-agent LangGraph workflow that separates the tasks of cited fact collection, reasoning over cited facts, and policy-oriented synthesis. Using a small, reproducible benchmark labeled as answerable or unanswerable, and considering two operating modes (analysis and policy), the multi-agent workflow reduces the proportion of unsupported claim units from 58.73% to 36.78% and improves refusal precision from 0.00% to 66.67%. However, it also exhibits citation index drift, which reduces citation accuracy from 87.50% to 62.50%. These results highlight both the value of architectural guardrails and the need for automated citation validation and repair in multi-step generation.

title: PORTRAIT: a calibrated patient ‘Passport’ with built-in refusal - describing individuals against a reference population
authors: Daniela Oehring
abstract: Abstract Background Average-based summaries serve individual patients poorly. PORTRAIT is a calibrated, abstention-aware tool that describes where one patient sits relative to a reference population across 12 cardiometabolic markers, how confident that placement is, and which features drive it. PORTRAIT describes; it does not diagnose or predict. Abstention is a designed feature given the known limits of conditional coverage. Methods Conformal calibration was combined with distribution-free coverage bounds, quantile-regression coordinates, and copula-based joint structure. A frozen reference cohort (n=9421) supplied fixed calibration; a held-out cohort (n=2247) tested transportability across six strata. A release gate required the minimum per-slice coverage to hold across 4 of 5 seeds. Coverage was re-tested under survey weighting to the US adult population. Coherence was reported as a descriptive joint coordinate. Discrimination was summarised with Harrell’s C and multiplicity controlled by BH-FDR. Interface conformance was assessed against defined requirements, Nielsen heuristics, and WCAG 2.2 AA, with attention to automation bias and risk-graph design. Results Estimating the conformal quantile once on the deep frozen reference held all six strata within band (0.864-0.903) at abstention 0.113, whereas a local re-split - calibrating each stratum on far fewer rows - under-covered to 0.71 at abstention 0.227; the difference is a calibration-depth effect, and coverage survived survey weighting. The release gate passed on 4 of 5 seeds at abstention 0.101 against a nominal 0.90, and in the frozen-reference configuration that ships, all six strata held inside the calibrated band (0.864-0.903). Coherence showed orthogonality 0.444 to raw extremity and correlated 0.892 with a copula-Mahalanobis distance while remaining deliberately non-identical, so it adds per-feature information. Two transfer tests returned negatives; the ocular transfer did not hold coverage at thin-n. Adding coherence changed mortality discrimination by deltaC 0.0047. Interface requirements moved from 14/27/18 to 38/14/7 (MET/PARTIAL/UNMET); Nielsen severity resolved 7 of 10 issues; WCAG 2.2 AA text criteria passed. Conclusions PORTRAIT situates a patient against a frozen reference, holds coverage under survey weighting to the US adult population, and abstains when calibration cannot be supported. The headline result is a calibration-depth effect: estimating the conformal quantile once on the deep frozen reference held per-stratum coverage on a disjoint cohort. Lay summary Blood tests are usually read one line at a time, each result checked against a normal range. Two things slip through this net. First, every result can sit inside its own normal range while the combination is genuinely unusual - a pattern no single line flags, so it is never investigated. For the patient that can mean real symptoms left unexplained and a problem recognised later than it should have been: dangerous, not merely inconvenient. Second, when a combined risk score does raise a concern, it rarely shows which results caused it, so a clinician cannot see what to act on. Neither failure is visible on the screen that produced it - nothing tells the reader that something has been missed. This matters more now that patients can see their own results and, increasingly, paste them into general-purpose artificial-intelligence tools for an interpretation. Those tools return a confident answer whether or not it is justified, and the more markers a person has, the harder the whole picture is to make sense of. PORTRAIT is built to do the opposite. For one person it describes where each result sits against a large, fixed reference population and how sure that placement is, reporting a range rather than a bare number. It flags which results are surprising given the rest, so the reasons behind a concern are never lost. It gives a single read of how unusual the whole profile is when the results are taken together. And, unlike the displays a clinician sees today, it knows when to stay silent: where a lab report or growth chart shows one line at a time and a risk score gives one number with no breakdown, none of them can tell that the reference population cannot support a reliable statement about a particular person. PORTRAIT refuses in exactly those cases and says so plainly, rather than producing a confident-looking result that is not backed by evidence. The result is designed to be read on a single page and used in a hospital, a general practice, or a high-street setting, with a plain-language mode for the people whose results are being described. Every statement it makes is checked for calibration against a fixed reference population, and it refuses when that check cannot be met. Looking forward, the same signals that mark a profile as surprising when its results are read together are being examined against real health outcomes, to test whether these patients differ in ways that current displays cannot see.
